title: Kestrel Logistics landing zone Terraform stubs and operational notes
body:
Summary:
This is a working draft for Kestrel Logistics' private deployment landing zone. Goal: produce a minimal, auditable VPC + cluster landing zone (AWS-first with on-prem hybrid notes) and a small set of Terraform stubs that Kestrel can run during the cutover window. This document captures architecture constraints, sizing assumptions, recommended TF module shapes, a short upgrade strategy for future model/quant changes, and operational run notes for cutover.

Context and constraints:
- Customer: Kestrel Logistics (global freight operator), strict data residency; primary region: us-east-1, DR in eu-west-1.
- Security: must integrate with Kestrel's existing AWS org and centralized logging (CloudWatch/Elasticsearch hosted by them). No managed NATs allowed; central egress proxy required.
- Connectivity: Private link to Kestrel's on-prem data center via Transit Gateway + VPN, variable latency between 15-80ms depending on site.
- SLA: target p95 latency for inference <200ms for 2k TPS burst workloads to route planner service.
- Compliance: audit logs to customer KMS; HSM integration optional for key wraps.

Assumptions used for sizing and choices:
- Typical model: 7B dense model quantized to int8 during deploy; per-request average tokens generated 128.
- Expected steady-state QPS: 250 RPS (peak 2,000 RPS bursts). Estimated 10 concurrent streams per GPU when batching optimized; target 12-14 max per GPU when using continuous batching windows.
- Preferred instance family: p4d-like or equivalent A100 40GB for hosted heavy throughput; fallback to A10G/RTX6000 for cost tier.
- Autoscaling window tolerance 90s for burst absorb; cold-starts must be avoided for traffic-critical routes.
- Network MTU and jumbo frames available on customer side for inter-node RPC.

Recommended high-level architecture (short):
- Landing zone components: shared VPC (control plane peering), workload VPCs per environment (prod/staging), Transit Gateway attachment for on-prem connectivity, central NAT/Egress-proxy in shared services account, Kinesis/Firehose for telemetry to customer's logging account.
- Cluster: containerized inference runtime on EC2 GPU instances behind a private ALB. Autoscaling group sized by GPU counts with node labels for model family.
- Storage: S3 in customer account for model artifacts + EFS for small persistent caches. Put model caches on NVMe local ephemeral where applicable.
- KMS: bring-your-own-KMS per customer requirement; Terraform must allow optional HSM-backed key_id input.

Terraform module notes (stubs & requirements):
- Naming guidance: modules must be short and composable. Proposed modules: "landing_zone_network", "shared_services", "gpu_node_pool", "model_registry_s3", "iam_bindings", "transit_gateway_attachment".
- Variables to include (minimal):
  - landing_zone_network: region, cidr_primary, cidr_private_subnets (list), az_count, enable_flow_logs (bool), tenant_tag_map (map)
  - shared_services: account_id, egress_proxy_ami (opt), kms_key_id (opt), logging_bucket_name
  - gpu_node_pool: instance_type_list (list), gpu_count_per_node (number), desired_capacity, max_capacity, boot_volume_size_gb, gpu_taints (list)
  - model_registry_s3: bucket_name, lifecycle_policy (string), kms_key_id
  - transit_gateway_attachment: tgw_id, vpn_config (map), static_routes (list)
- Outputs to expose: vpc_id, private_subnet_ids (list), alb_sg_id, node_iam_role_arn, autoscaling_group_name
- Implementation notes: modules should emit tags for billing/cost center, accept map of extra_tags. Keep provider configurations in root module to allow account-level switches.

Terraform practical stubs to include in delivery package (what we'll hand off):
- terraform/root/main.tf: provider config, backend s3 (customer), workspace hints.
- terraform/modules/landing_zone_network/{main.tf,variables.tf,outputs.tf}: skeleton for subnets, route tables, flow logs.
- terraform/modules/gpu_node_pool/{main.tf,variables.tf,outputs.tf}: launch template referencing customer AMI, user_data placeholder to pull runtime container image.
- terraform/env/prod/variables.tfvars.example: values for CIDRs, account ids, model bucket name.

Operational notes for cutover (sequence):
1) Preflight: validate TF plan in staging account with identical CIDR/account scoping. Run "terraform plan" and produce drift report.
2) Networking: create Transit Gateway Attachment and confirm BGP/route propagation to on-prem. Verify ICMP and SSH to bastion hosts.
3) Security: provision KMS keys and validate encrypt/decrypt by node IAM role. Confirm CloudTrail events flow to customer's account.
4) Model sync: push a single model artifact to S3 (signed) and perform a dry-run serving test on a small cold pool of 2 GPUs.
5) Scale test: synthetic load up to 25% of target burst to validate batching and KV cache warmup.
6) Cutover: progressively increase traffic via weighted routing (50/50 for 15m) then 90/10 for 10m before full shift.

Upgrade path notes (model/quant/serving runtime):
- Rolling upgrade recommended. Strategy: build new AMI/container with runtime + new quant libs, deploy new node pool with scale-up then cordon+drain old nodes. Estimate time 20-40 minutes per AZ for safe drain with slow connection sites.
- Fall back: keep a compatible 8-bit variant of the model in S3 and provide traffic-split failover policy in the YAML routing layer.

Architecture Q&A (customer-facing prompts and answers):
Q: Can we keep models inside our VPC only?
A: Yes. Model artifacts stay in S3 in the customer's account; runtime nodes fetch with VPC endpoints (s3 gateway). If stricter network egress is required, pre-populate local NVMe cache via rsync to avoid S3 calls after cutover.

Q: What happens when GPUs require driver upgrades?
A: Driver/kernel upgrades require node replacement. Use a staged AMI bake + new node pool method. We recommend a canary AZ test before full roll.

Q: How do we validate cost during initial run?
A: Enable per-node metrics and token-level cost proxy in the runtime. We will provide a small script to estimate token cost vs GPU-hour.

Open questions (to resolve with Kestrel):
- Final list of on-prem sites that will call the inference endpoint and their expected latencies.
- Confirmation whether they will accept single-account landing zone or prefer cross-account shared services.
- KMS/HSM procurement timeline and whether we should plan for HSM at first deploy.

Cutover checklist (quick actionable items):
- [ ] TF backend bucket access granted to redwood-infra-bot
- [ ] TGW peering IPs and BGP info from Kestrel network ops
- [ ] KMS key ARN and policy snippet for node role
- [ ] Sample model artifact (signed) for smoke test
- [ ] Logging/alerting subscription configured in customer account

Notes to engineering team (internal):
- Keep modules intentionally small; avoid heavy provider-specific logic. Acceptability matrix: if a customer wants GCP/Azure hybrid, we will add provider-agnostic inputs but core VPC design remains AWS-first for this engagement.
- Provide a small acceptance test harness (go binary + k6 script) to run scale test that reports back to our monitoring.

Action items (owners):
- Marco: create TF root skeleton and backend config by 2026-03-17
- Sana: build the initial GPU node user_data snippet with runtime startup logging by 2026-03-20
- Aisha: coordinate network preflight with Kestrel netops and produce TGW plan by 2026-03-15

Appendix: small capacity calculation example (summary)
- Target burst = 2k RPS, avg tokens per request = 128 -> tokens/s = 256k tokens/s
- If model throughput per A100 ~ 20k tokens/s at target latency, GPUs needed ~ 13 (rounded to 16 to allow headroom and AZ distribution)
- Steady-state of 250 RPS -> tokens/s = 32k tokens/s -> GPUs needed ~ 2 (use small pool + scale policy).

This is a working draft. Expect follow-ups after the network topology confirmation and KMS decision.

Notes to self: keep the module var names snake_case for easier compatibility with the customer's existing TF repos.
